pages.title: Learn
pages.headline: Make sense of digital trust.
pages.excerpt: Explore wallets, credentials and the roles behind them. Follow a knowledge route at your own pace, or bring your team to a guided session.

pages.title: Topics
pages.headline: Choose what you want to understand.
pages.excerpt: Start with the big picture or go straight to a question. There is no required sequence and no account is needed.

pages.title: The big picture
pages.excerpt: Before choosing a wallet or a standard, understand what needs to be trusted — and who can provide the evidence.

pages.title: For businesses
pages.excerpt: Start with a business process: what must your organisation prove, receive or check?

pages.title: Ecosystem roles
pages.excerpt: A wallet interaction involves several parties. One provides information, another holds it, and a service requests and checks it. Providers and trust services may support the process.

pages.title: The holder
pages.excerpt: A holder receives a credential and can present information from it to another party. The holder may be a person using a personal wallet or an organisation using a wallet in a business process.
pages.sources:
W3C · Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0 | https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/
European Commission · Selective disclosure of attributes in the EUDI Wallet | https://ec.europa.eu/digital-building-blocks/sites/spaces/EUDIGITALIDENTITYWALLET/pages/949256476/What%2Bis%2Bselective%2Bdisclosure%2Bof%2Battributes

pages.title: The issuer
pages.excerpt: An issuer provides a credential containing information about a person, organisation or another subject. A school can issue a qualification, for example, or an organisation can issue evidence that a person holds a particular role.
pages.sources: W3C · Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0 | https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/

pages.title: The relying party
pages.excerpt: A relying party is an organisation or service that requests and uses information from a wallet. An employer checking a qualification is one example. The organisation needs to decide what information it needs and what it will use it for.
pages.sources:
W3C · Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0 | https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/
European Commission · Selective disclosure of attributes in the EUDI Wallet | https://ec.europa.eu/digital-building-blocks/sites/spaces/EUDIGITALIDENTITYWALLET/pages/949256476/What%2Bis%2Bselective%2Bdisclosure%2Bof%2Battributes

pages.title: Wallet providers and other service providers
pages.excerpt: A wallet provider makes a wallet available to people or organisations. The wallet helps its users receive, manage and present information. Other providers may supply software or services to the organisations that issue or check that information.

pages.title: Trust service providers and trust frameworks
pages.excerpt: Digital interactions often involve several organisations. A trust service provider can provide services that help parties establish or check aspects of a digital interaction. A trust framework sets out agreements and rules for participants in a particular ecosystem.
pages.sources:
European Commission · EU trusted lists | https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/eu-trusted-lists
European Commission · Questions and answers on trust services under the European digital identity regulation | https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/questions-answers-trust-services-under-european-digital-identity-regulation

pages.title: For governments
pages.excerpt: Public organisations meet wallets from two sides: they hold information people need to prove, and they run services that need to receive it. Start with the question closest to yours.

pages.title: Digital wallets and public services
pages.excerpt: People regularly have to show public services information that a public body holds. Where could a wallet fit next to the ways they already do that?
